text: Your first flow. Here's a real request: when a new Incident comes in marked Priority 1, Critical, send a notification to the manager of the group it gets assigned to, so they know immediately without watching the queue. Your job is to translate that plain-language request into a trigger and a sequence of actions.

This is a reaction to something happening, not a periodic job, so it's a Record trigger, not a Scheduled one. You set the table to Incident, the change type to Created rather than Updated, because this is about catching the Incident the moment it's new. Then you add the condition that narrows it down: Priority is 1, Critical. Without that condition, the flow fires on every new Incident, not just the ones that matter.

Next, you add the built-in Notify action. Instead of typing in a fixed recipient, you reference a data pill from the trigger — the triggering Incident's Assignment Group, and from there, that group's manager. That's a dynamic reference that resolves differently for every Incident. You'd also pull in the Incident's number and short description so the message is actually useful.

A newly built flow saves in an inactive state — it won't run against real records yet. Saving preserves your work; activating is the separate, deliberate step that turns the trigger engine on. Once you're confident the trigger and the Notify action are configured correctly, you activate it, and every new Priority 1 Incident now triggers a notification automatically.

Nothing in this flow required a line of JavaScript — just a trigger, a condition, and one action, built entirely from the last three lessons. Chapter 2 starts right where this left off: data pills, the mechanism that let the Notify action reach into the triggering record in the first place.
